appraisal_events.evidence: « Tu sais, j'ai raconté à Bloch, me dit Saint-Loup, que tu ne l'aimais pas du tout tant que ça... Voilà comme je suis, j'aime les situations tranchées », conclut-il d'un air satisfait ; « il l'avait trahie par ce qu'il avait dit à Bloch » ; « une expression hideuse de bassesse, presque de bestialité ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator, whose judgment the passage plainly endorses, treats Saint-Loup's self-satisfied disclosure as a betrayal of loyal friendship and reads it in his face as an eclipse of his own self by an ancestral baseness, sharply lowering him.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Les idées qui m'étaient apparues s'enfuirent... dès qu'on est deux elles disparaissent... Et je me trouvai rejeté dans l'amitié » ; « un enthousiasme qui aurait pu être fécond si j'étais resté seul, et m'aurait évité ainsi le détour de bien des années inutiles ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The retrospective narrator diminishes his own evening by showing that Saint-Loup's companionship drives off the visionary ideas that would have disclosed his vocation, so that the comfort of friendship is bought at the cost of wasted years.

status_effects.explanation: Saint-Loup falls clearly in this passage: his warm arrival is overtaken by an act the narrator calls a betrayal, delivered with vulgar self-satisfaction and marked by a physiognomy of hideous baseness.
The narrator gains a brief comfort from Saint-Loup's entrance, but ends stupefied by the betrayal and stripped of the ideas he could only have had alone; the local balance is a loss.

Saint-Loup speaks « sur un ton qui n'admettait pas de réplique » and the narrator's intended rebuke stays unspoken, leaving him silenced within the scene even though he wins the judgment in narration.

ambiguities: Saint-Loup's arrival is described in strongly positive terms (« une arrivée de bonté, de gaieté, de vie »), but it is framed inside a long devaluation of friendship as a « breuvage funeste » of mediocre pleasure, so whether he is locally elevated at all before the betrayal is genuinely underdetermined; it is read here as qualified relief rather than a positive movement.

The narrator explicitly leaves Saint-Loup's motive open (embarrassment, unconsciousness, stupidity, passing ill humor toward himself or toward Bloch); the condemnation is unambiguous, but the cause of the act is not, which limits how far the diminishment can be read as characterological rather than momentary.
